situations.name: Adding a background loop
situations.definition: A developer needs a new piece of work to run repeatedly forever in the app process, with a cadence, a panic boundary, health metrics, and a way to stop it.
situations.note: 37 loops implement ReactiveSubscription and get panic-catching, backoff, idle cadence, leadership gating and health metrics for free; ~8 more hand-roll tokio::spawn + interval and get none of it. The trait exists and is documented as 'no new tokio::spawn block needed' — the divergence is that nobody enforces it.

situations.name: Cross-process loop ownership
situations.definition: Deciding which of several processes sharing one local DB (windowed app, headless daemon, test instance) is allowed to run a singleton loop.
situations.note: Two independent lease mechanisms coexist — engine-leader.lock (any instance) and daemon.lock (trigger-kind ownership, checked separately in should_yield_to_daemon). Getting it wrong double-fires every schedule and double-rotates OAuth against one SQLite file.

situations.name: Loop restart safety
situations.definition: Making sure starting or restarting the scheduler cannot leave a second live copy of every loop running against the same data.
situations.note: Dropping a JoinHandle does NOT abort a tokio task, so a bare `running: bool` lets orphaned loops resurrect on the next start. Solved by a monotonic generation counter + a CAS on start — a non-obvious answer that any new loop author would get wrong by default.

situations.name: Atomic job claim
situations.definition: Taking exclusive ownership of a queued row / key so exactly one worker acts on it, even with overlapping ticks, multiple processes, or a restart mid-flight.
situations.note: Three different mechanisms: guarded SQL UPDATE (claim_pending, claim_continuation), an in-memory InflightGuard/HashSet slot, and a lock file. Choosing wrong is silent — an in-memory guard cannot represent 'still running' once the fire path returns (documented explicitly at background.rs:2188).

situations.name: Reaping stranded work
situations.definition: Returning rows stuck in a non-terminal state (claimed-but-never-finished, running-but-dead) to the queue or to a terminal status without stealing work from a healthy worker.
situations.note: Each reaper invents its own staleness proof: two-consecutive-snapshot sets for events, a wall-clock threshold for zombie executions, heartbeat silence for the passive watchdog, task-handle absence for assignments. No claim timestamp exists to lean on, which is exactly why the two-pass hack is needed.

situations.name: Boot crash recovery
situations.definition: Deciding, at app start, what to do with rows the last process left mid-flight so no work is lost and no dead work looks alive.
situations.note: The subtle rule is per-status: `running` rows must be failed (their subprocess is gone) but `queued` rows must be re-admitted (they are durable work). A prior version failed both and silently dropped every scheduled execution waiting at shutdown.

situations.name: Scheduled trigger firing
situations.definition: Evaluating cron/interval schedules on a tick and publishing exactly the right fires, including catching up slots missed while the app was closed.
situations.note: Backfill is the hard part: per-trigger cap AND a global per-tick cap are both needed or a mass restart after downtime becomes a thundering herd. curation_scheduler deliberately does NOT share the abstraction, which is a documented fork worth revisiting.

situations.name: Spawning a CLI subprocess
situations.definition: Launching an external binary (Claude CLI, git, an MCP server, a verification command) with the right env, working dir, window flags, stdin delivery and kill semantics.
situations.note: Windows binary resolution alone has four fallback layouts (cli_process.rs:52). The stdin-writer-must-be-detached pipe-deadlock rule, CREATE_NO_WINDOW, kill_on_drop and env stripping are each re-derived at call sites that bypass the helper.

situations.name: One-shot headless LLM call
situations.definition: Sending one prompt to the model from Rust and getting text or JSON back, without the full persona execution pipeline.
situations.note: THE worst divergence in the slice: three competing envelopes (spawn_headless_claude for stream-json, run_claude_cli for plain -p -, run_claude_prompt_text_inner living in a commands module the engine imports upward). Each has its own timeout, model pin, turn cap and auth handling. The doc comment on spawn_headless_claude records that some call sites previously forgot force_subscription_auth and silently billed the API account.

situations.name: Streaming model output
situations.definition: Reading a model's NDJSON stream line by line, turning lines into typed events, and acting on them while the run is still in flight.
situations.note: MAX_LINE_BYTES truncation, subagent attribution via parent_tool_use_id, and a post-mortem re-parse for messages missed mid-stream are all non-obvious requirements. The HTTP engine reimplements the same shape for a different wire format.

situations.name: Prompt assembly
situations.definition: Building the full prompt for a run from persona config, tools, memory, connector hints, protocol contracts and mode directives.
situations.note: Four compilers share Compile/Chain vocabulary and duplicated parsing until a README + a compile-time PROMPT_ASSEMBLY_INVENTORY assertion was added to stop a fifth appearing silently. That guard is the interesting answer, not the prompt text.

situations.name: Structured output extraction
situations.definition: Getting a reliable typed value out of free-form model text that may be fenced, prefixed, truncated or malformed.
situations.note: safe_json::lenient_from_str exists and is the right answer, but extract_fenced_block, extract_first_json_object, and per-module DIRECTOR_VERDICT/protocol regex scrapers all coexist. Size/nesting DoS limits live only in safe_json, so the hand-rolls have no bound.

situations.name: LLM contract enforcement
situations.definition: Making the system behave correctly when the model ignores a rule the prompt stated — synthesizing the missing step, blocking bad output, or scoring it.
situations.note: gates.rs states the general truth plainly: 'Sonnet 4.x treats the rule as advisory', so Rust must enforce and synthesize a fallback. Everywhere else the app still trusts the prompt. This is the situation most likely to be re-derived badly by a new feature.

situations.name: Model and effort routing
situations.definition: Deciding which model, effort tier and provider a given call should use, given persona config, policy, capability and per-use-case overrides.
situations.note: A four-level specificity cascade exists (explicit profile > persona rule > category rule > universal), plus BYOM policy, plus per-capability defaults, plus a remote-HTTP fork keyed on the provider string. Headless helpers bypass all of it and hardcode a model literal.

situations.name: Provider failover
situations.definition: Detecting a retryable provider failure and moving the same run to the next model/provider candidate without failing it.
situations.note: Two circuit breakers exist in the app (provider-level here, persona-level in healing_orchestrator) with no shared state and documented independent reset paths — a genuine trap for anyone adding a third.

situations.name: Healing strategy selection
situations.definition: Choosing what happens after a run fails: retry with backoff, resume the session and let the model fix itself, roll back, or disable the persona.
situations.note: The precedence is explicit and the mutual-exclusion invariant is subtle: AI healing and auto-rollback write the SAME two prompt columns, so they share the healing_personas slot. The module doc records that the earlier 'different levels, therefore safe' reasoning was simply false.

situations.name: Retry with backoff
situations.definition: Re-attempting a failed operation on a delay that grows, is capped, and does not storm a failing dependency.
situations.note: At least seven independent exponential-backoff implementations with different bases, caps, eviction policies and persistence (in-memory map with TTL+LRU in polling, DB ledger in oauth_refresh, per-loop counter in subscription, sleep-doubling in persist). No shared primitive exists at all.

situations.name: Timeout tiering
situations.definition: Choosing the timeout for an operation so that inner timeouts surface useful errors before outer ceilings kill the process.
situations.note: The ordering constraint is real and load-bearing (DEFAULT_EXECUTION_TIMEOUT_MS is 11min specifically to sit above the CLI's own 10min subagent-stall cutoff, guarded by a unit test), but the other ~15 timeouts are unrelated magic constants with no stated relationship to each other.

situations.name: Cancellation and teardown
situations.definition: Stopping in-flight work on demand: flagging it, killing child processes, letting metrics flush, and cleaning every registry entry.
situations.note: Four mechanisms in play: AtomicBool flags, kill_process on a tracked PID, tokio CancellationToken, and the ProcessSession/ActiveProcessRegistry contract. The 5-second grace window has to re-check the PID map afterwards because a chain retry can spawn a NEW child during the grace period — an orphan that keeps spending.

situations.name: Admission control and queueing
situations.definition: Deciding whether a newly requested run starts now, waits in a priority queue, or is rejected — under per-entity and global limits.
situations.note: ConcurrencyTracker is the canonical answer for persona executions, but it stacks three orthogonal admission gates (per-persona max_concurrent, global cap, quota cooldown, resource-governor pause) and needed its own QueueDrainWatchdog because a stuck gate silently means nothing runs.

situations.name: Keyed rate limiting
situations.definition: Capping how often an operation may run per key over a sliding window, and telling the caller when to retry.
situations.note: RateLimiter is shared by the two tool surfaces, but api_proxy has its own token bucket and polling.rs has its own failure backoff map. Bucket pruning, warn-once latching and empty-bucket edge cases were all learned once and not shared.

situations.name: Emitting to the frontend
situations.definition: Pushing a typed payload from an engine module to the React UI so a surface updates live.
situations.note: Three layers claim ownership — the typed event_registry, the headless-safe ExecutionEventEmitter trait, and ~90 raw app.emit(...) calls (some with a module-local event-name const, e.g. kb_extract's PROGRESS_EVENT, which the TS registry never sees). The registry's stated 5-step 'adding an event' ritual is widely skipped.

situations.name: Publishing a domain event
situations.definition: Recording something that happened as a persona_event so triggers, feeds, healing and the UI can all react to it.
situations.note: Event names drift in separator style because some are LLM-emitted (`code_review.completed` vs `code-review.completed`), which forced canonical matching downstream. There is also an unwritten rule that some event types are informational-only (never listener-matched, so they never spawn a run) with no type-level marker.

situations.name: Event to subscriber matching
situations.definition: Deciding which personas/triggers a published event should wake, and recording why a match did NOT produce a run.
situations.note: The EventGateReason token ledger exists because every gate used to `continue` silently, leaving a NULL error_message and no way to say why a trigger didn't fire. Wildcard source_filter also needs a cross-team bleed guard. Both are the kind of thing a new matcher would omit.

situations.name: External source ingestion
situations.definition: Bringing events in from a third-party system — polling an API, holding an SSE/websocket relay, or draining a cloud queue — into the local bus.
situations.note: Every ingestor re-invents cursor/watermark storage, dedup, reconnect backoff, buffer caps and 'forward-only, never backfill the whole table' semantics. webhook_notifier documents the watermark-seeding trap in detail; nothing generalizes it, so the next connector will hit it again.

situations.name: Multi-step orchestration
situations.definition: Driving a graph of dependent steps — topological order, per-step status, conditional edges, cascade-skip on failure, and a terminal rollup.
situations.note: Four independent DAG drivers: pipeline_executor (team pipeline graph), team_assignment_orchestrator (step DAG with review pause), chain.rs (event cascade with depth limit), build_session (turn/fan-out graph). They agree on nothing — status vocabulary, parallelism budget and failure semantics all differ.

situations.name: Bounded parallel fan-out
situations.definition: Running N independent sub-tasks at once with a concurrency budget, isolating a panic in one, and collecting results in order.
situations.note: run_lanes is a clean, tested primitive explicitly built to be reused — and is still marked #![allow(dead_code)] 'wired in Phase 3'. Meanwhile the assignment orchestrator hand-rolls max_parallel_steps. Whether the fan-out is in-process, subprocess, or subagent (parent_tool_use_id) changes the answer completely.

situations.name: Human-in-the-loop gates
situations.definition: Pausing autonomous work for a person to decide, keeping the paused state durable, and resuming exactly once when they answer.
situations.note: Five different pause surfaces (manual_reviews, awaiting_review on a step, pipeline approval gate, capability gate state machine, evolution promotion proposal) with five different resume paths. Only incident_continuation states an at-most-once resume guarantee; the others rely on UI discipline.

situations.name: Token and cost accounting
situations.definition: Capturing what a model call actually cost and attributing it to the run, persona, and aggregate that has to answer for it.
situations.note: Two truths coexist: measured cost from the CLI result event, and an estimator (cost.rs) with hardcoded per-model list prices and CHARS_PER_TOKEN = 3.8 that silently defaults unknown models to Sonnet pricing. Nothing reconciles them, and headless helper spawns record no cost at all.

situations.name: Aggregate spend ceiling
situations.definition: Bounding total cost across an operation that spawns the model many times, not just per individual call.
situations.note: The design doc is blunt: --max-budget-usd binds per spawn only, so evolution (15-25 spawns), lab matrix and pipelines could quietly cost N x a single run. The RunBudgetLedger is a launch gate, not a kill switch, and is warn-only by default. Meanwhile schedule_over_budget, enclave max_cost_usd and fix_loop max_attempts are four unrelated ceilings.

situations.name: Credential injection into a child
situations.definition: Getting a decrypted secret out of the vault and into a spawned process's environment safely, refreshing OAuth first if needed.
situations.note: Well-owned: one denylist (BLOCKED_ENV_NAMES), one sanitizer, a per-credential refresh mutex so concurrent runs don't burn each other's grant, zeroize on drop, and a hard-fail gate (no partial fallback). The divergence risk is the zero-plaintext broker path, which is a completely different model for the same goal.

situations.name: Billing-account auth enforcement
situations.definition: Guaranteeing every spawned model process authenticates against the intended account, never silently falling back to metered API billing.
situations.note: Small surface, maximal consequence: three env vars, stripped in three spawn paths. The doc comment records that before force_subscription_auth was folded into the shared spawn, some call sites forgot it and the user was silently billed pay-as-you-go. Any fourth spawn path re-opens the hole.

situations.name: SSRF-safe outbound HTTP
situations.definition: Calling a URL supplied by a user, a connector config, or the model itself without letting it reach private/internal/metadata addresses.
situations.note: Two answers coexist: build_ssrf_safe_client (custom DNS resolver, closes the TOCTOU/rebinding window) and validate_url_safety (a pre-check that mcp_tools.rs:1409 explicitly notes is TOCTOU-vulnerable on its own). http_engine has a third, its own is_blocked_ip. Which one you need is not obvious from the call site.

situations.name: Tool invocation result contract
situations.definition: Returning a tool call's outcome in a shape callers, the audit log and the incidents inbox can all reason about, with output bounded.
situations.note: A good example of a solved situation: three encodings of failure were unified into one typed ToolErrorKind + classify_app_error. Worth codifying because the persona LLM tool path deliberately does NOT flow through it, which is easy to misread as an omission.

situations.name: Warm session and result caching
situations.definition: Avoiding repeated setup cost by keeping a subprocess, session, or prepared payload alive between calls, with correct invalidation.
situations.note: Four hand-rolled caches, each with its own TTL, size cap and eviction (30min config-hash-keyed session pool, 5min/64-entry prepared run cache, 60s MCP tools/list TTL, auto-prune-every-100-calls rate buckets). The invalidation key is the hard part and differs every time.

situations.name: Session resume and continuation
situations.definition: Continuing a prior model conversation rather than starting cold — for retries, healing, fix loops, or context carry-over between runs.
situations.note: Whether to resume is decided in at least four places with different rules — session pool TTL+config hash, healing 'resume the original session', backoff retries deliberately restart fresh, fan-out deliberately uses a fresh temp dir with NO --continue. The cost/coherence tradeoff is never stated in one place.

situations.name: Deterministic verification and fix re-entry
situations.definition: Running a real check (tests, lint, exit code) after a model run and looping it back with the failure, bounded so it cannot spin.
situations.note: Newer and cleanly factored (decision core / command runner / signature breaker are three separate pure modules), but opt-in and OFF by default. The safety posture — bounded attempts, a normalized failure signature so an identical deterministic failure stops the loop — is the transferable answer.

situations.name: Burst debounce and episode dedup
situations.definition: Collapsing a flood of near-identical signals into one action, and announcing a state crossing exactly once instead of on every occurrence.
situations.note: Five distinct dedup strategies: coalesce-by-path + time window (file watcher), durable episode row (SLA), stable source_id so incidents fold into one open row, a warn-once latch (rate limiter), and 'fold further losses into the open healing issue'. Each was learned independently.

situations.name: Stall and liveness watchdogs
situations.definition: Detecting that something which should be making progress has gone quiet, and raising a visible, deduped signal instead of failing silently.
situations.note: Every watchdog was added reactively after a specific incident (the module doc names a 2-day silent fleet deadlock). Each defines its own silence threshold, its own evidence query and its own alerting channel; there is no template for 'this subsystem needs a watchdog' at design time.

situations.name: Durable terminal-state persistence
situations.definition: Writing an operation's final status so it is never lost, never overwrites a status a racing path already wrote, and dead-letters if the DB is unavailable.
situations.note: Two variants matter and the distinction is easy to miss: persist_status_update (retry then dead-letter) vs persist_status_if_running (guarded so a cancel cannot clobber a completed status the run already wrote).

situations.name: Autonomy gating
situations.definition: Answering 'may this autonomous action run right now, for this project?' before spending money or mutating state unattended.
situations.note: Recently unified: ~15 global autonomous_* booleans plus a per-project autopilot enum used to make every read site re-derive precedence inline. The single rule (explicit project row wins in BOTH directions, else global flag) is now in one module — but every new autonomous subscription must remember to ask it.

situations.name: Retention and pruning
situations.definition: Keeping high-volume tables and in-memory maps from growing without bound, without deleting rows something still needs.
situations.note: Seven independent retention policies — a settings-driven day count for events (with its own unparseable-value warn path), hardcoded 7 days for project events, TTL+LRU for backoff maps, TTL+size cap for the prepared-run cache. Retention exempting in-flight rows is what created the stranded-event bug in the first place.

situations.name: Cross-device job dispatch
situations.definition: Accepting and running work sent from another machine, deciding whether the sender is allowed to make you run anything.
situations.note: The load-bearing distinction is stated once and nowhere else: an AUTHENTICATED peer is not a TRUSTED one. The handshake proves identity; a separate owned_devices gate decides who may run instructions. The management_api Bearer-key route is the same situation over HTTP with a different answer.

situations.name: Agent workspace isolation
situations.definition: Giving an agent run a working directory and a way to undo what it did there, without letting it reach outside.
situations.note: The exec dir is per-persona and deliberately persistent (so sidecar config and on-disk work survive between runs), which is the opposite of the fan-out path's fresh-temp-dir rule. Checkpointing exists only for the dev-tools plugin; ordinary executions have no rewind.

situations.name: Pre-flight dependency validation
situations.definition: Proving before a run starts that everything it needs — credentials, connectors, peer personas, capability contracts — actually exists.
situations.note: The point is turning execution-time cryptic failure into design-time visibility. healthcheck's three-state outcome (verified / cannot-probe / failed) is the same lesson from the credential side — a binary success flag lied about unprobeable credentials.
